To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
epiphyseal age assessment of the radius and third metatarsal can be used as a valid method to estimate the age of a person in criminal proceedings.

the ossification of the epiphyyses in the hand skeleton of living subjects can be classified into five stages, and that the ossification stage 5 (absent epiphyseal line) of the epiphyses of radius and third metatarsal is a potential parameter for determining a minimum age of living subjects of 18 year.
ossification stages 4 and 5 of selected epiphysis of the hand skeleton are age-independent and therefore not suitable for age estimation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of a new method for the age estimation of living persons.
the question of how far the ossification of the epiphysis of the third metacarpus and of the phalanges of the hand can be used as an indicator of age.
a possible expansion of the ossification stage classification system for the hand skeleton.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ossification stage of the epiphyses of radius, ulna and third metacar-pal is a useful parameter in the assessment of the age of the living person in the age range 10–18 years.

the ossification stage of the hand skeleton can be used to estimate the minimum age of a living person with a high level of reliability and accuracy, and that the ossification of the radius is the most reliable parameter for this purpose.
the age of the hand skeleton can be estimated by the ossification of selected hand epiphyses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ossification of the epiphysea of the hand skeleton can be used to estimate the age of living subjects in criminal proceedings.
the ossification of the epiphyses of selected elements of hand skeleton is a useful additional tool for age estimation in living subjects.

epiphyseal age determination of the hand is not a valid tool to determine the age of a living individual in criminal proceedings, but it can be a helpful tool in forensic age diagnostics for the estimation of the minimum age in cases of missing persons.
The main takeaway from our work is that

epiphyseal stages of the radius, third metacarpals and basal phalanges can be used to determine a minimum age in living subjects with an error margin of ± 0.8 years in males and ± 0.9 years in females.
epiphyseal age assessment in the hand can provide valuable additional information for age estimation in living subjects.
the ossification stage of epiphyses of certain hand bones can be used to estimate the minimum age in forensic age diagnostics.
